strengths: The paper identifies an important and under-discussed practical issue in off-policy learning for large action spaces: optimizing common IPS-style OPL objectives can be much harder than evaluating their statistical properties would suggest.

The oracle-policy analysis is useful for clarifying the implicit biases of IPS, cIPS, ES, DR, MIPS, OffCEM, POTEC, PC, and PWLL-style objectives, and it gives a coherent rationale for objective-aware policy parameterizations.

The connection between PWLL/reward-weighted behavioral cloning and better-conditioned optimization is clearly presented. The concavity result for linear-softmax policies is simple but relevant, and the paper is careful to state that PWLL is not a new method.

The empirical section covers large nominal action spaces across three recommendation datasets and includes several useful stress tests: batch size and scheduler sensitivity, seed variance, reward noise, support size, smaller action spaces, clustering sensitivity, and pessimistic regularization baselines.

The limitations section honestly notes that PWLL is not an OPE estimator, cannot directly solve policy selection, depends on logging-policy coverage, and loses formal concavity guarantees for end-to-end deep policies.
weaknesses: The central claim that optimization matters more than estimation is overgeneralized relative to the evidence. The experiments are semi-synthetic recommender evaluations with a constructed logging policy and held-out interaction rewards, not real logged bandit deployments or online validation. This setting may favor behavior-cloning-style methods because the logging policy and evaluation construction are both derived from the same collaborative-filtering embeddings/history split.

The action-space scale claim is somewhat confounded: although the nominal action spaces are 60K to 1M, the default logging support is only k0=100 per context. The strongest objective-aware results restrict the effective action space to this support, so the practical comparison is partly about support truncation and candidate generation rather than optimizing over truly million-action feasible supports.

The theoretical contribution is mostly worst-case and adapted from existing softmax optimization results. The plateau result is an existence result with O(Keff) iterations, and the exponential-local-maxima statement is imported via Chen et al. with little detail about whether the assumptions match the paper's estimator classes and parameterizations. These results support plausibility, but they do not by themselves establish that the observed empirical gaps are caused by the stated optimization pathologies.

The comparison between estimation accuracy and policy quality is not fully convincing. The MSE definition and evaluation protocol are not described in enough detail in the main text, PWLL methods are excluded from the MSE plots because they are not value estimators, and lower OPE MSE not correlating with learned reward among a few IPS variants does not cleanly prove that estimation quality is less important than optimization.

Baseline tuning and reproducibility details are incomplete. The appendix mentions Adam, one-cycle schedules, batch-size sweeps, and tuned configurations, but does not give enough concrete hyperparameters, learning rates, model dimensions, optimizer settings, or selection rules to independently assess fairness. The claimed public code/artifact footnote appears empty in the extracted manuscript.

The empirical baselines may be disadvantaged by using generic softmax/embedding parameterizations and limited training details. Since the paper's thesis is about optimization, stronger optimizer baselines, alternative parameterizations, longer training budgets, candidate-sampling approximations, or direct optimization diagnostics would be important to rule out implementation-specific failures.

The paper's originality is moderate. PWLL/reward-weighted likelihood methods are well known in offline RL and imitation-style policy improvement, and the paper acknowledges this. The main novelty is the large-action OPL diagnosis and synthesis, which is useful but currently not supported strongly enough for the breadth of the conclusions.

The impact statement is perfunctory for a recommender-system paper. Since the methods directly target recommendation and offline policy learning from biased logs, a more substantive discussion of exposure bias, feedback loops, user welfare, and deployment risks would be appropriate.

strengths: The paper raises a useful and practically important point: in large-action offline contextual bandits, optimizing IPS-style OPL objectives can be as important as, or more important than, estimator variance/MSE. This is a worthwhile corrective to an estimator-centric literature.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is not convincingly supported. The experiments are based on recommender-style semi-synthetic logged data where the logging policy, embeddings, contexts, and rewards are constructed from the same interaction matrix, and validation reward is held-out membership rather than a true counterfactual policy value. This makes it hard to conclude that PWLL would genuinely outperform IPS-based OPL in real logged bandit deployments.

strengths: The paper makes a useful and timely point: in large-action offline contextual bandits, the optimization landscape of OPL objectives can be as important as, or more important than, the statistical quality of the corresponding OPE estimator. This is a valuable corrective to an estimator-centric literature.

The oracle-policy analysis is clear and helpful. Characterizing the asymptotic maximizers of IPS, clipped IPS, ES, DR, MIPS, OffCEM, POTEC, PC, and PWLL variants gives concrete insight into the inductive biases of these objectives and motivates objective-aware parametrizations.

The PWLL discussion is well positioned: the authors do not overclaim algorithmic novelty, and instead argue that reward-weighted log-likelihood objectives are optimization-friendly alternatives for policy learning. The concavity result for linear-softmax policies is simple but important, and the connection to stochastic optimization guarantees is convincing under the stated assumptions.

The empirical study is unusually large for this area, covering MovieLens with 60k actions, Twitch with 200k actions, and GoodReads with 1M actions. The optimization stress tests over batch sizes, learning-rate schedules, seeds, reward noise, logging support size, number of clusters, and pessimistic regularization provide substantial evidence for the central qualitative claim.

The paper is generally well written and candid about limitations: PWLL is not an OPE estimator, cannot directly support policy selection by value estimation, depends on logging-policy support, and loses formal concavity guarantees for end-to-end deep training.
weaknesses: The main claim is somewhat broader than the evidence supports. The experiments show that PWLL-style objectives are strong in the authors' semi-synthetic recommender setup, but this does not fully establish that optimization generally matters more than estimation in large-action OPL. The conclusion should be framed more carefully as evidence for this regime rather than a general principle.

The evaluation relies on logged recommendation datasets converted into an offline bandit problem with synthetic logging policies and held-out-item rewards. This is a reasonable stress test, but it may favor objectives that stay close to the logging-policy support or exploit the same embeddings used to construct the logging policy. More diverse environments or real logged propensities would strengthen external validity.

Important optimization-friendly baselines are missing or underemphasized. Since PWLL is compared mainly against IPS-style estimators, it would be useful to include stronger direct-method or supervised reward-model policies, especially because large-scale recommendation systems often use such approaches and they are also easier to optimize than IPS objectives.

The theoretical results for IPS optimization pathologies are mostly existential and adapted from prior work. They convincingly explain possible failures, but they do not tightly characterize when the empirical failures should occur in the studied recommender settings. Some propositions are also stated at a high level in the main text, with important conditions only clarified in the appendix.

The comparison between estimator MSE and learned-policy quality is suggestive but not fully decisive. PWLL objectives are not value estimators, so their high MSE is not very informative; within IPS methods, lower MSE not predicting better reward supports the authors' point, but a more systematic analysis of estimation error versus optimization error would make the argument stronger.

Reproducibility is promising because the paper claims public code and gives many implementation details, but the manuscript excerpt does not provide a clearly visible artifact URL or enough detail to independently verify all preprocessing, tuning ranges, and selection rules. The results also rely heavily on figures, with relatively few tabulated numerical values for exact comparison.

The impact statement is generic. The paper concerns recommender systems and offline optimization from biased logs, so risks around feedback loops, exposure bias, and deployment of policies learned from historical user behavior deserve at least brief discussion.
